chapters.title: Gravitation
chapters.description: Concept of gravitational force, Newton’s law of gravitation, Kepler’s laws, free fall, acceleration due to gravity, escape velocity, and weightlessness.
learningObjectives: Explain Newton’s universal law of gravitation.
Apply Kepler’s laws to planetary motion.
Differentiate between mass and weight.
Solve numerical problems based on gravitational force and free fall.
Define escape velocity and weightlessness.

questions.text: State Newton’s universal law of gravitation.
questions.answer: According to the law, every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

questions.text: Which force is responsible for circular motion of a stone tied to a string rotating in a horizontal circle?
questions.answer: Centripetal force

questions.text: State Kepler’s second law of planetary motion and explain its meaning.
questions.answer: Kepler’s second law states that the line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. This means planets move faster when closer to the Sun and slower when farther away.

questions.text: Two masses of 10 kg and 20 kg are placed 2 m apart. Calculate the gravitational force between them. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ Nm²/kg².
Explain how Kepler’s third law helped Newton derive the inverse square law of gravitation.
questions.answer: Kepler’s third law states that T² ∝ r³. Using circular motion, centripetal force F = mv²/r and v = 2πr/T. Substituting these into the equation shows that F ∝ 1/r², indicating that the gravitational force decreases with the square of distance.

questions.text: The value of acceleration due to gravity ‘g’ is highest at:
questions.answer: Poles

questions.text: What is free fall?
questions.answer: When an object moves only under the influence of gravitational force, it is said to be in free fall.

questions.text: A stone is dropped from a height of 80 m. Calculate the time taken to reach the ground. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: Using s = ½gt² → 80 = 5t² → t² = 16 → t = 4 s.

questions.text: Define escape velocity and state its value on Earth.
questions.answer: Escape velocity is the minimum velocity required for an object to escape Earth’s gravitational pull without falling back. For Earth, it is 11.2 km/s.

questions.text: Explain the concept of weightlessness in spacecraft.
questions.answer: Space travellers appear weightless because spacecraft and everything inside it are in free fall under Earth's gravity. Since all fall with the same acceleration, no normal force acts on the astronauts, making them feel weightless.

questions.text: What is free fall? When does it occur?
questions.answer: Free fall is the motion of a body under the influence of gravitational force alone. It occurs when no other force acts on the body.

questions.text: State Newton’s universal law of gravitation. What happens to gravitational force when (a) distance is tripled (b) mass of one body is doubled?
questions.answer: Force is inversely proportional to square of distance and directly proportional to product of masses. If distance is tripled, force becomes 1/9. If mass is doubled, force doubles.

questions.text: A satellite orbits at a height of 35780 km above earth with velocity 3.08 km/s. Find the time period of revolution. (Radius of earth = 6400 km)
questions.answer: Orbital circumference / velocity gives time period ≈ 24 hours.

questions.text: An iron ball of mass 3 kg is released from a height of 125 m. Assuming g = 10 m/s², find (a) time taken to reach the ground (b) velocity on reaching the ground.
questions.answer: Time = 5 s, velocity = 50 m/s.

questions.text: Distinguish between mass and weight.
questions.answer: Mass is constant and measured in kg; weight depends on gravity and measured in newton.

chapters.title: Periodic Classification of Elements
chapters.description: Classification of elements, Dobereiner’s triads, Newlands’ law of octaves, Mendeleev’s periodic table, and the evolution of modern periodic classification.
learningObjectives: Explain why elements are classified.
Describe Dobereiner's triads with examples.
State Newlands’ law of octaves and identify its limitations.
Explain the construction and advantages of Mendeleev’s periodic table.
Apply periodic classification to compare element properties.

questions.text: What were Dobereiner’s triads? Give one example.
questions.answer: Dobereiner classified elements into groups of three with similar properties, where the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the mean of the other two. Example: Li (6.9), Na (23), K (39.1).

questions.text: According to Newlands’ law of octaves, the properties of elements repeat after:
questions.answer: Every 8th element

questions.text: State Newlands’ law of octaves and mention one limitation.
questions.answer: Newlands stated that when elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic mass, every eighth element shows properties similar to the first. Limitation: The law was applicable only up to calcium and could not accommodate newly discovered elements.

questions.text: Explain how Mendeleev arranged the elements in his periodic table.
questions.answer: Mendeleev arranged 63 elements in increasing order of atomic mass and grouped them based on similarities in the chemical and physical properties of their oxides and hydrides.

questions.text: Which property did Mendeleev consider fundamental while preparing the periodic table?
questions.answer: Atomic mass

questions.text: Write two achievements of Mendeleev’s periodic table.
questions.answer: 1. It predicted the existence and properties of undiscovered elements. 2. It grouped elements with similar properties together and corrected wrong atomic masses.

questions.text: Why could Newlands not include noble gases in his law of octaves?
questions.answer: Noble gases had not been discovered at the time, and their later inclusion disturbed the arrangement because they appeared after every seven elements.

questions.text: Discuss the limitations of Mendeleev’s periodic table.
questions.answer: 1. Position of hydrogen was uncertain as it resembled both alkali metals and halogens. 2. Increasing atomic mass did not always match with chemical properties, causing element reversal (e.g., Co and Ni). 3. No place for isotopes since they have identical properties but different masses. 4. The table could not fully explain the structure of atoms.

questions.text: Compare Dobereiner’s triads, Newlands’ octaves, and Mendeleev’s periodic table.
questions.answer: Dobereiner grouped elements in triads based on atomic mass mean values. Newlands arranged elements in increasing atomic mass and observed repetition every eighth element. Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass but grouped them by chemical properties, predicting new elements and correcting atomic masses.

questions.text: Explain how Mendeleev predicted the existence of undiscovered elements.
questions.answer: While arranging elements, Mendeleev noticed gaps where no known element fit the expected chemical properties. He left these gaps and predicted elements like eka-silicon and eka-aluminium, describing their properties accurately before their discovery.

questions.text: State Dobereiner’s law of triads with one example.
questions.answer: Elements arranged in triads have atomic mass of middle element equal to average of other two. Example: Li, Na, K.

questions.text: Complete the paragraph on classification of elements based on electronic configuration.
questions.answer: Elements are classified into four blocks: s, p, d and f blocks with metals, non-metals and metalloids accordingly.

questions.text: Name the atom having the smallest atomic size.
questions.answer: Helium.

questions.text: Alkaline earth metals have valency 2. Their position in the modern periodic table is in:
questions.answer: Group 2

questions.text: Name the element: (a) most electronegative atom (b) atom with smallest atomic mass (c) noble gas with smallest atomic radius.
questions.answer: (a) Fluorine (b) Hydrogen (c) Helium.

questions.text: Atomic number of chlorine is 17. Write its electronic configuration, valence electrons, molecular formula, type of bond and draw electron-dot structure.
questions.answer: Electronic configuration: 2,8,7; valence electrons: 7; molecular formula: Cl₂; bond: covalent.

chapters.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chapters.description: Types of chemical reactions, balancing equations, oxidation-reduction, and identification of chemical change.
learningObjectives: Write and balance chemical equations.
Differentiate between various types of chemical reactions.
Identify oxidation and reduction processes.
Explain displacement, decomposition, and combination reactions.
Interpret chemical change through observations.

questions.text: Define a chemical reaction with one example.
questions.answer: A chemical reaction is a process in which reactants convert into products with new chemical properties. Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.text: Which of the following is a decomposition reaction?
questions.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

questions.text: Why do chemical equations need to be balanced?
questions.answer: Chemical equations must be balanced to follow the law of conservation of mass, which states that matter cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

questions.text: Which of the following reactions is a redox reaction?
questions.answer: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu

questions.text: State any two observations that indicate a chemical reaction is taking place.
questions.answer: 1. Formation of precipitate. 2. Change in color. 3. Evolution of gas. 4. Change in temperature.

questions.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction between aluminium and oxygen.
questions.answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

questions.text: What is oxidation? Give one example.
questions.answer: Oxidation is the process in which a substance gains oxygen or loses electrons. Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

questions.text: Explain displacement and double displacement reactions with suitable examples.
questions.answer: In displacement reactions, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. Example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. In double displacement reactions, ions of two compounds exchange places to form new compounds. Example: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl (ppt) + NaNO₃.

questions.text: Describe the various types of chemical reactions with one example each.
questions.answer: 1. Combination: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. 2. Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 3. Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. 4. Double displacement: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl. 5. Redox reactions: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

questions.text: Explain reduction with an example.
questions.answer: Reduction is the process in which a substance loses oxygen or gains electrons. Example: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, where CuO is reduced to Cu.

questions.text: Write the molecular formula of calcium carbonate.
questions.answer: CaCO₃

questions.text: What are the factors affecting the rate of chemical reaction?
questions.answer: Nature of reactants, concentration, temperature, catalyst and surface area.

questions.text: Observe the given reaction setup and answer related questions.
questions.answer: Effervescence is due to CO₂; lime water turns milky; sodium carbonate can be replaced by sodium bicarbonate.

questions.text: The reaction in which ions are exchanged to form a precipitate is called:
questions.answer: Double displacement

questions.text: What happens when copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid? Write the balanced equation.
questions.answer: Brown NO₂ gas is released. Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.text: What is meant by decomposition reaction? Write the reaction of decomposition of sugar on heating.
questions.answer: A reaction in which a compound breaks into simpler substances. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O.

chapters.title: Effects of Electric Current
chapters.description: Heating, magnetic and chemical effects of electric current, electric power, electric circuits and applications.
learningObjectives: Explain heating, magnetic, and chemical effects of electric current.
Apply Joule’s law to calculate heat produced.
Describe working of electromagnets and electric motors.
Interpret magnetic field patterns around conductors.
Solve numericals based on electric power and electrical energy.

questions.text: State Joule’s law of heating.
questions.answer: Joule’s law states that the heat produced in a conductor is directly proportional to the square of the current, resistance of the conductor, and time: H ∝ I²Rt.

questions.text: What happens when an electric current flows through a conductor?
options: Both heat and magnetic field are produced
questions.answer: Both heat and magnetic field are produced

questions.text: Calculate the heat produced when a 2 A current flows through a 5 Ω resistor for 10 seconds.
questions.answer: Using H = I²Rt → H = (2²)(5)(10) = 200 J.

questions.text: State the right-hand thumb rule.
questions.answer: If the right-hand thumb points in the direction of current, the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field around the conductor.

questions.text: An electromagnet is stronger when:
options: A soft iron core is used
It is kept in a wooden frame
questions.answer: A soft iron core is used

questions.text: What is the chemical effect of electric current? Give one application.
questions.answer: When an electric current passes through a conducting solution, chemical reactions occur. Example: Electroplating.

questions.text: Define electric power and write its SI unit.
questions.answer: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or converted. Its SI unit is watt (W).

questions.text: Explain the working of an electric motor using the magnetic effect of current.
questions.answer: Electric motors work on the principle that a current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field. A rectangular coil placed between magnet poles rotates when current flows through it due to the force on its arms. A commutator reverses the current every half turn, ensuring continuous rotation.

questions.text: Describe the magnetic field produced around a straight conductor and a solenoid.
questions.answer: A straight conductor produces concentric circular magnetic field lines around it. A solenoid produces a uniform magnetic field inside, similar to a bar magnet, with a north and south pole. The field strength increases with increased current and number of turns.

questions.text: A device consumes 1000 W of power and operates for 3 hours. Calculate the electrical energy consumed in kWh.
questions.answer: Energy = Power × Time = 1000 W × 3 h = 3 kWh.

questions.text: Why tungsten is used to make filament in electric bulbs?
questions.answer: Tungsten has very high melting point and emits light without melting.

questions.text: What is a solenoid? Draw a neat labelled diagram.
questions.answer: A solenoid is a coil of insulated copper wire producing magnetic field when current flows.

questions.text: Which material is used to make solenoid type coil in an electric bulb?
questions.answer: Tungsten

questions.text: Why copper or aluminium wires are used for electric power transmission?
questions.answer: They have low resistivity and high electrical conductivity.

chapters.title: Heat
chapters.description: Temperature, modes of heat transfer, latent heat, specific heat capacity, calorimetry, and change of state.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between heat and temperature.
Explain conduction, convection, and radiation.
Define specific heat capacity and latent heat.
Solve numerical problems based on heat calculations.
Explain real-life applications of heat transfer.

questions.text: What is specific heat capacity?
questions.answer: Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C.

questions.text: Which mode of heat transfer does NOT require a medium?
questions.answer: Radiation

questions.text: Differentiate between heat and temperature.
questions.answer: Heat is a form of energy transferred due to temperature difference, while temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.

questions.text: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 20°C to 40°C? (Specific heat of water = 4200 J/kg°C)
What is latent heat of fusion?
questions.answer: Latent heat of fusion is the heat absorbed by a solid to convert into a liquid at constant temperature.

questions.text: Convection occurs mainly in:
questions.answer: Liquids and gases

questions.text: Explain why cooking takes longer at high altitudes.
questions.answer: At high altitudes, atmospheric pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature. Since the temperature is lower, food takes longer to cook.

questions.text: Explain conduction, convection, and radiation with examples.
questions.answer: Conduction: Heat transfer through solids without movement of particles, e.g., a metal rod heated at one end. Convection: Heat transfer by movement of particles in liquids/gases, e.g., water heating in a vessel. Radiation: Heat transfer through electromagnetic waves, e.g., heat from the Sun.

questions.text: How much heat is required to convert 500 g of ice at 0°C into water at 0°C? (Latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg)
Describe the working principle of a calorimeter.
questions.answer: A calorimeter works on the principle of conservation of energy. It measures heat exchange between substances placed inside it. Its insulating walls prevent external heat loss, allowing accurate measurement of heat gained or lost by materials.

questions.text: The SI unit of heat is:
questions.answer: Joule

questions.text: Write the use of calorimeter.
questions.answer: To measure quantity of heat exchanged.

questions.text: Name and state the principle used to measure the specific heat capacity of a substance.
questions.answer: Principle of calorimetry: heat lost equals heat gained.

questions.text: Name the behaviour of water between 0°C and 4°C.
questions.answer: Anomalous expansion of water.

chapters.title: Refraction of Light
chapters.description: Refraction through plane surfaces, laws of refraction, refractive index, optical density, and real-life applications.
learningObjectives: State and explain the laws of refraction.
Define refractive index and calculate its value.
Explain optical density and its effect on refraction.
Describe refraction through a glass slab and real-life examples.
Solve numerical problems involving refractive index and velocity of light.

questions.text: What is refraction of light?
questions.answer: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another due to a change in its speed.

questions.text: Which quantity determines how much the light bends during refraction?
questions.answer: Refractive index

questions.text: State Snell’s law of refraction.
questions.answer: Snell’s law states that the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media: sin i / sin r = constant = n.

questions.text: If the refractive index of water is 1.33, find the speed of light in water. (Speed of light in air = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Explain optical density and how it affects the speed of light.
questions.answer: A medium with higher optical density slows down light more than a medium of lower optical density. Light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium.

questions.text: When a ray of light travels from glass to air, it bends:
questions.answer: Away from the normal

questions.text: What is meant by apparent depth?
questions.answer: Due to refraction, an object in a denser medium appears to be raised when viewed from a rarer medium. This apparent shift is called apparent depth.

questions.text: Explain refraction through a glass slab using a ray diagram and describe lateral shift.
questions.answer: When light enters a glass slab, it bends towards the normal due to higher density. On emerging, it bends away from the normal, making emergent ray parallel to the incident ray. The perpendicular distance between the emergent and incident rays is called lateral shift.

questions.text: Describe real-life applications of refraction with at least three examples.
questions.answer: Examples include: 1) Apparent bending of a stick in water. 2) Formation of mirages. 3) Lenses used in spectacles and cameras. 4) Twinkling of stars due to atmospheric refraction.

questions.text: A ray of light enters a medium with angle of incidence 30° and angle of refraction 20°. Calculate the refractive index of the second medium.
We can see the sun even when it is below the horizon due to:
questions.answer: Refraction of light

questions.text: Observe the dispersion diagram and answer related questions.
questions.answer: Violet deviates most, red least; rainbow is natural example; spectrum is band of colours.

questions.text: Light changes direction when going from one medium to another. This is called:
questions.answer: Refraction

questions.text: What is the reason for twinkling of stars?
questions.answer: Atmospheric refraction.

questions.text: Explain the formation of rainbow with a neat labelled diagram.
questions.answer: Rainbow is formed due to refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection in water droplets.

chapters.title: Lenses
chapters.description: Types of lenses, refraction through lenses, sign conventions, lens formula, magnification, and applications.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between convex and concave lenses.
Draw ray diagrams for image formation by lenses.
Use lens formula and magnification formula.
Explain real-life applications of lenses.
Solve numerical problems involving lenses.

questions.text: What is a convex lens?
questions.answer: A convex lens is a transparent optical device that is thicker at the center than at the edges and converges incoming parallel rays to a point.

questions.text: Which lens diverges parallel rays of light?
questions.answer: Concave lens

questions.text: State the lens formula and explain each term.
questions.answer: The lens formula is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u, where f = focal length, v = image distance, and u = object distance.

questions.text: An object is placed 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance.
Explain the sign convention used for lenses.
questions.answer: All distances are measured from the optical center. The direction of incident light is positive. Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative. Heights above the principal axis are positive, below are negative.

questions.text: A concave lens always forms:
questions.answer: Virtual and erect image

questions.text: What is magnification? Write its formula.
questions.answer: Magnification is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object. m = h₂/h₁ = v/u.

questions.text: Describe image formation by a convex lens when the object is placed beyond 2F.
questions.answer: When the object is beyond 2F, the image is formed between F and 2F, real, inverted, and smaller in size. Ray diagram: 1) A ray parallel to principal axis passes through F. 2) A ray through optical center continues straight without deviation.

questions.text: Calculate the power of a lens of focal length +50 cm.
questions.answer: P = 1/f (in meters) → f = 0.50 m → P = 1/0.50 = +2 diopters.

questions.text: Explain the working of a compound microscope.
questions.answer: A compound microscope uses two convex lenses—the objective lens and eyepiece. The objective lens forms a magnified real image of the object near its focus. The eyepiece further magnifies this image, producing a highly enlarged virtual image.

questions.text: Which lens is used in a simple microscope?
questions.answer: Convex

questions.text: The focal length of a convex lens is 20 cm. Find its power.
questions.answer: Power = +5 dioptre.

questions.text: Match: Simple microscope — used to observe minute objects.
questions.answer: Simple microscope → observe minute objects.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of human eye and answer related questions.
questions.answer: Diagram drawn correctly; minimum distance of distinct vision is 25 cm; defect is presbyopia.

chapters.title: Metallurgy
chapters.description: Occurrence of metals, concentration of ore, extraction processes, refining methods, and applications of metals.
learningObjectives: Explain the terms mineral, ore, and metallurgy.
Describe various methods of concentration of ore.
Explain extraction steps for metals of different reactivity.
Differentiate between roasting and calcination.
Describe refining methods and real-life applications.

questions.text: What is an ore?
questions.answer: An ore is a naturally occurring mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently.

questions.text: Which process is used to remove impurities lighter than the ore?
questions.answer: Froth flotation

questions.text: Differentiate between minerals and ores.
questions.answer: Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic compounds of metals. Ores are minerals from which extraction of metal is economically feasible.

questions.text: What is roasting?
questions.answer: Roasting is a process in which sulphide ores are heated in the presence of air to convert them into oxides.

questions.text: Highly reactive metals like sodium and aluminium are extracted by:
questions.answer: Electrolysis

questions.text: Explain calcination with one example.
questions.answer: Calcination is the heating of an ore in the absence of air to remove water or volatile impurities. Example: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.

questions.text: Name the three steps in metallurgy.
questions.answer: 1. Concentration of ore, 2. Extraction of metal, 3. Refining of metal.

questions.text: Describe the electrolytic extraction of aluminium.
questions.answer: Aluminium is extracted from alumina (Al₂O₃) using electrolysis. Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower melting point. In the electrolytic cell, aluminium is deposited at the cathode, while oxygen is released at the carbon anode, which gradually burns away.

questions.text: Explain the process of refining by electrolysis.
questions.answer: In electrolytic refining, the impure metal is used as the anode and the pure metal as the cathode. The electrolyte contains a salt solution of the metal. Impure metal dissolves from the anode and deposits pure metal on the cathode, leaving impurities as sludge.

questions.text: Describe the extraction of iron from its ore in the blast furnace.
questions.answer: Iron is extracted from hematite in a blast furnace. Coke acts as a reducing agent, limestone removes impurities as slag, and hot air supports combustion. Iron oxide is reduced to molten iron, which collects at the bottom, while slag floats on top.

questions.text: In which process molten tin is deposited on metals?
questions.answer: Tinning

questions.text: Why silver articles turn black on exposure to air?
questions.answer: Due to formation of silver sulphide.

questions.text: What is done to prevent rusting of iron doors?
questions.answer: Painting, galvanizing or oiling.

questions.text: Name two metals which can be cut with a knife.
questions.answer: Sodium and potassium.

chapters.title: Carbon Compounds
chapters.description: Covalent bonding, versatile nature of carbon, homologous series, functional groups, nomenclature, and chemical properties of carbon compounds.
learningObjectives: Explain the covalent bonding in carbon compounds.
Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Identify functional groups and name organic compounds.
Understand homologous series and its characteristics.
Describe chemical reactions involving carbon compounds.

questions.text: What are hydrocarbons?
questions.answer: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds composed only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an alkene?
questions.answer: C₂H₄

questions.text: What is a homologous series? State one characteristic.
questions.answer: A homologous series is a group of organic compounds having the same functional group and general formula. Consecutive members differ by −CH₂− and show a gradual change in properties.

questions.text: Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
questions.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons have only single bonds (alkanes), while unsaturated hydrocarbons contain double or triple bonds (alkenes and alkynes).

questions.text: Which functional group is present in alcohols?
questions.answer: –OH

questions.text: Name the following compound: CH₃–CH₂–COOH
questions.answer: Propanoic acid

questions.text: Explain the versatile nature of carbon.
questions.answer: Carbon is versatile due to catenation (ability to form long chains), tetravalency, ability to form strong covalent bonds, and formation of various structures like rings and branched chains.

questions.text: Describe the chemical properties of ethanol.
questions.answer: 1. Combustion: Ethanol burns to form CO₂ and water. 2. Reaction with sodium: Produces sodium ethoxide and hydrogen. 3. Dehydration: Ethanol forms ethene in presence of concentrated H₂SO₄.

questions.text: Write the molecular formula for the 4th member of the alkene series.
questions.answer: General formula for alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ → For n = 4: C₄H₈.

questions.text: Explain esterification with a chemical equation.
questions.answer: Esterification is the reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water. Example: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

questions.text: Which functional group belongs to carboxylic acid?
questions.answer: –COOH

questions.text: Write any three general properties of ionic compounds.
questions.answer: High melting point, soluble in water, conduct electricity in molten state.

questions.text: Why ethanol is added to petrol in some countries?
questions.answer: To increase combustion efficiency and reduce pollution.

questions.text: Name the non-metal which is a good conductor of electricity.
questions.answer: Graphite.

chapters.title: Space Missions
chapters.description: Evolution of space missions, satellites, launch vehicles, Indian space programs, and applications of satellites.
learningObjectives: Explain different types of satellites and their uses.
Describe the working and purpose of launch vehicles.
Understand PSLV and GSLV technologies.
Describe major achievements of India in space exploration.
Explain applications of artificial satellites.

questions.text: What is an artificial satellite?
questions.answer: An artificial satellite is a man-made object placed in orbit around Earth or another celestial body for communication, research, weather forecasting, and other purposes.

questions.text: Which of the following is a launch vehicle developed by ISRO?
questions.answer: PSLV

questions.text: Differentiate between geostationary and polar satellites.
questions.answer: Geostationary satellites orbit Earth at 36,000 km and appear stationary relative to Earth, used for communication. Polar satellites orbit over poles at low altitudes and cover the entire Earth, used for weather and mapping.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a launch vehicle?
questions.answer: A launch vehicle is used to carry a satellite or spacecraft into space by overcoming Earth’s gravitational force using high thrust engines.

questions.text: Which of the following satellites is used for weather forecasting?
questions.answer: INSAT

questions.text: What is PSLV? Mention one of its achievements.
questions.answer: PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) is an ISRO-developed launch vehicle known for launching satellites into polar orbits. It successfully launched 104 satellites in a single mission in 2017.

questions.text: Explain any two applications of artificial satellites.
questions.answer: 1. Communication: TV, internet, telephone signals. 2. Navigation: GPS and location services. 3. Weather forecasting: Predicting natural disasters. 4. Earth observation: Mapping and resource management.

questions.text: Explain the working principle of a geostationary satellite with a diagram.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite orbits Earth at 36,000 km in the equatorial plane, completing one revolution in 24 hours. Thus, it appears fixed over one point on Earth. It constantly relays signals for communication. Its orbital speed matches Earth’s rotational speed.

questions.text: Describe the features and significance of India’s Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan).
questions.answer: Mangalyaan was India's first interplanetary mission launched in 2013. It made India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit and the first in the world to do so on its first attempt. It studied Martian atmosphere, surface features, and captured high-resolution images.

questions.text: Explain GSLV and how it differs from PSLV.
questions.answer: GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) uses a cryogenic upper stage and is designed to launch heavier satellites into geostationary orbits. PSLV is used mainly for launching lighter satellites into polar orbits. GSLV has higher payload capacity and uses more advanced propulsion.

questions.text: What is meant by satellite launch vehicle? Name any one Indian SLV.
questions.answer: A vehicle used to place satellites into orbit. Example: PSLV.

questions.text: Complete the table showing types of satellites, their function and Indian satellite series with launch vehicles.
questions.answer: Navigation satellite – fixes location – IRNSS – PSLV; Weather satellite – INSAT.

questions.text: Rocket is a type of fire cracker. Name the launcher and the law on which it works.
questions.answer: Launcher: tube; Law: Newton’s third law of motion.

chapters.title: Heredity and Evolution
chapters.description: Heredity, genes, transcription–translation, mutation, evolution, Lamarckism, Darwin’s theory, speciation, and human evolution.
learningObjectives: Explain the mechanisms of heredity and gene expression.
Describe transcription, translation, and mutation.
State major theories and proofs of evolution.
Differentiate Lamarckism and Darwinism.
Understand speciation and human evolutionary history.

questions.text: What is heredity?
questions.answer: Heredity is the transfer of biological characters from one generation to the next through genes. Genes present on chromosomes carry this information.

questions.text: Which molecule carries the genetic information required for protein synthesis?
questions.answer: DNA

questions.text: What is transcription?
questions.answer: Transcription is the process in which mRNA is synthesized from the DNA template. Only one strand of DNA is used, and uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

questions.text: Explain translation and translocation in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Translation is the process by which tRNA brings amino acids to the mRNA codons to form proteins. Ribosomes move one codon at a time along mRNA—this movement is called translocation.

questions.text: Which scientist proposed the theory of natural selection?
questions.answer: Darwin

questions.text: What is mutation? Give an example.
questions.answer: Mutation is a sudden change in the nucleotide sequence of a gene. Example: mutation causing sickle cell anaemia.

questions.text: Differentiate between Lamarckism and Darwinism.
questions.answer: Lamarckism states that acquired characters are inherited, while Darwinism states that natural selection allows organisms with favorable variations to survive and reproduce.

questions.text: Explain the evidences of evolution with examples.
questions.answer: Evidences include morphological similarities (e.g., leaf venation, mouthparts), anatomical evidences (similar bone structure in human hand, bat wing, whale flipper), vestigial organs (appendix, body hair), fossil records showing gradual development, and embryological similarities. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Explain speciation. How does geographical isolation contribute to it?
questions.answer: Speciation is the formation of new species from an existing one when populations accumulate genetic variations over time. Geographical isolation prevents interbreeding, leading to independent evolution and formation of new species. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}

questions.text: Describe the evolution of modern humans.
questions.answer: Human evolution began around 7 crore years ago with lemur-like ancestors. Ape-like ancestors evolved into Dryopithecus, Ramapithecus, Australopithecus, and then upright man. Neanderthal and Cro-Magnon humans followed. Homo sapiens evolved around 50,000 years ago, developed tools, agriculture, and civilizations. :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}

questions.text: A minor change occurring due to change in position of any nucleotide is termed as:
questions.answer: Mutation

questions.text: Define vestigial organs. Write names of any two vestigial organs in human body.
questions.answer: Vestigial organs are reduced and functionless organs. Examples: appendix, coccyx.

questions.text: Explain the following terms: (a) Stem cells (b) Cloning (c) Genetically modified crops.
questions.answer: Stem cells can differentiate into various cell types; cloning produces genetically identical organisms; GM crops have altered genes for desired traits.

questions.text: Any nucleotide of the gene suddenly changes its position that causes a minor change is called:
questions.answer: Mutation

questions.text: Study of fossils is an important aspect of the study of evolution.
questions.answer: True

questions.text: Define heredity. Explain the mechanism of hereditary changes.
questions.answer: Heredity is the transmission of genetic characters from parents to offspring. Hereditary changes occur due to mutation, recombination and chromosomal changes.

chapters.title: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part - 1
chapters.description: Human organ systems, energy production, respiration, digestion, circulation, excretion, and control systems.
topics: Role of digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems
Cell division as a life process
learningObjectives: Explain the interdependence of organ systems in the human body.
Describe digestion, respiration, circulation and excretion.
Understand ATP generation and cellular energy production.
Explain the role of control systems such as the nervous and endocrine system.
State the importance of cell division in life processes.

questions.text: What is the importance of a balanced diet for the human body?
questions.answer: A balanced diet provides all essential nutrients required for energy production, growth, repair, and proper functioning of body systems.

questions.text: Which cell organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.answer: Mitochondria

questions.text: What is respiration? How does it occur in the human body?
questions.answer: Respiration is the process of breaking down food to release energy. In humans, oxygen is taken in through breathing and transported to cells where it helps oxidize glucose to release ATP.

questions.text: Explain the role of digestive juices in digestion.
questions.answer: Digestive juices contain enzymes that break down complex nutrients like carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into simpler absorbable forms. They help in efficient nutrient absorption.

questions.text: Which system carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell of the body?
questions.answer: Circulatory system

questions.text: Why is oxygen essential for energy production in cells?
questions.answer: Oxygen is necessary for the oxidation of food molecules in mitochondria. This oxidation releases energy stored in food and converts it into ATP, the usable form of energy in cells.

questions.text: How are various functions occurring in the human body coordinated?
questions.answer: Functions of the body are coordinated by the nervous system and endocrine system, which regulate responses, maintain balance, and ensure proper functioning of organs.

questions.text: Explain the process of energy production inside cells.
questions.answer: Energy is produced in mitochondria during cellular respiration. Glucose and oxygen are transported to cells via the circulatory system. Inside mitochondria, glucose is oxidized to release ATP. This ATP powers metabolic processes essential for life.

questions.text: Describe the role of the circulatory system in energy production and waste removal.
questions.answer: The circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients to cells for ATP production. It also carries waste products like carbon dioxide and urea to excretory organs for removal. Thus it maintains cellular homeostasis.

questions.text: Explain why coordination between digestive, respiratory, and circulatory systems is essential for survival.
questions.answer: The digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system provides oxygen, and the circulatory system transports both to body cells. Only when all three systems work in coordination can cells produce ATP needed for survival. Failure in any one system affects the entire organism. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Regeneration occurs in:
questions.answer: Planaria

questions.text: What are vitamins? Classify them according to their solubility.
questions.answer: Vitamins are organic nutrients required in small amounts. They are fat-soluble and water-soluble.

questions.text: A molecule of glucose is completely oxidised in aerobic respiration to produce water and:
questions.answer: CO₂

questions.text: Sometimes higher plants and animals perform anaerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Due to insufficient oxygen supply during intense activity.

questions.text: Find the odd one out: Fragmentation, Regeneration, Budding, Fertilization.
questions.answer: Fertilization

chapters.title: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part - 2
chapters.description: Asexual and sexual reproduction, reproduction in plants and animals, fertilization, embryo development, cell division (mitosis & meiosis).
learningObjectives: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction.
Describe reproduction in plants and human beings.
Explain fertilization, embryo development and pregnancy.
Understand mitosis and meiosis with diagrams.
Explain how genetic continuity is maintained through cell division.

questions.text: What is asexual reproduction?
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction is a mode in which a single parent produces offspring without gamete formation. Offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

questions.text: Binary fission occurs in:
questions.answer: Amoeba

questions.text: State any two differences between asexual and sexual reproduction.
questions.answer: 1. Asexual reproduction involves one parent; sexual reproduction involves two. 2. Asexual offspring are identical; sexual reproduction produces genetically diverse offspring.

questions.text: What is fertilization?
questions.answer: Fertilization is the process of fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote, which develops into an embryo.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a method of asexual reproduction?
questions.answer: Pollination

questions.text: Explain budding with an example.
questions.answer: In budding, a new organism develops from a small outgrowth (bud) on the parent body. Example: Yeast reproduces by budding.

questions.text: What is the role of meiosis in sexual reproduction?
questions.answer: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number to half in gametes, ensuring that fertilization restores the diploid number, maintaining genetic stability across generations.

questions.text: Describe the process of reproduction in flowering plants.
questions.answer: Flowering plants reproduce sexually. Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma. Pollen tube carries male gametes to ovule. Fertilization forms a zygote, which becomes an embryo. Ovule forms seed and ovary becomes fruit. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Explain mitosis and its significance.
questions.answer: Mitosis is equational cell division producing two identical daughter cells. Stages include prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. It enables growth, repair, and replacement of cells while maintaining chromosome number. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}

questions.text: Describe the process of human reproduction from gamete formation to embryo development.
questions.answer: Gametes form through meiosis. During fertilization, sperm fuses with ovum to form a zygote. The zygote undergoes mitosis to form a blastocyst, which implants in the uterus. It develops into an embryo supported by placenta and continues growth during pregnancy. :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}

questions.text: Answer the following questions based on human male reproductive system.
questions.answer: Sperms are formed in testes; length ≈ 60 µm; vas deferens transports sperms; sperms are formed by meiosis; unpaired organs: prostate gland, penis.

questions.text: In humans, sperm production occurs in:
questions.answer: Testes

questions.text: Being a fish, I perform respiration with the help of lungs. Who am I?
questions.answer: Lungfish

questions.text: Write any four stages of mitosis and explain any two of them.
questions.answer: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase. (Explanation of any two).

chapters.title: Environmental Management
chapters.description: Ecosystems, biodiversity, food chains, environmental conservation, waste management, pollution, and sustainable development.
learningObjectives: Explain the concept of ecosystems and biodiversity.
Identify types of pollution and their impact on the environment.
Describe food chains, webs, and trophic levels.
Understand methods of waste management and environmental conservation.
Explain sustainable development practices.

questions.text: What is an ecosystem?
questions.answer: An ecosystem is a system formed by the interaction between living organisms (biotic factors) and their physical environment (abiotic factors).

questions.text: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
questions.answer: Wind energy

questions.text: What is biodiversity? Why is it important?
questions.answer: Biodiversity refers to the variety of living organisms in an environment. It maintains ecological balance, provides resources, and supports ecosystem services.

questions.text: What is meant by sustainable development?
questions.answer: Sustainable development means fulfilling present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of biodegradable waste?
questions.answer: Kitchen waste

questions.text: Explain the term food chain with an example.
questions.answer: A food chain shows how energy flows from one organism to another. Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake.

questions.text: State two causes of air pollution.
questions.answer: Major causes include vehicle emissions, burning of fossil fuels, industrial smoke, and deforestation.

questions.text: What is waste management? Describe any two modern waste management techniques.
questions.answer: Waste management involves collection, treatment, and disposal of waste materials. Techniques include: 1. Composting—organic waste decomposed into manure. 2. Recycling—processing used materials into new products. 3. Vermiculture—using earthworms to convert waste into nutrient-rich compost.

questions.text: Explain the interrelationship between components of an ecosystem with examples.
questions.answer: Biotic and abiotic components interact to maintain balance. Plants depend on sunlight, water, and soil nutrients; herbivores depend on plants; carnivores depend on herbivores. Decomposers recycle nutrients back into the soil. These interactions create a stable ecosystem. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Describe major causes of environmental degradation and measures to prevent it.
questions.answer: Causes include pollution, overexploitation of resources, deforestation, and improper waste disposal. Preventive measures include afforestation, using renewable energy, reducing waste, pollution control technologies, and enforcing environmental laws. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}

questions.text: Write any four important facts which must be considered while planning disaster management.
questions.answer: Risk assessment, preparedness, mitigation measures, community participation.

questions.text: Redraw and complete the given chart related to environmental conservation.
questions.answer: Chart completed correctly showing conservation methods.

questions.text: What is biodiversity? Write any four steps to conserve biodiversity.
questions.answer: Biodiversity refers to variety of life forms. Conservation steps include afforestation, wildlife protection, pollution control and sustainable use.

questions.text: What are the constituents of acid rain? Write any two effects of acid rain.
questions.answer: SO₂ and NO₂; damages monuments and soil fertility.

chapters.title: Towards Green Energy
chapters.description: Conventional and non-conventional energy sources, solar energy, wind energy, hydroelectricity, biofuels, nuclear energy, and energy conservation.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between conventional and non-conventional energy sources.
Explain solar, wind, and hydroelectric energy generation.
Describe biomass, biogas, and biofuels.
Understand nuclear energy and its advantages and risks.
Explain the importance of energy conservation.

questions.text: What are non-conventional energy sources?
questions.answer: Non-conventional energy sources are renewable forms of energy such as solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, and biomass, which are environment-friendly and abundant.

questions.text: Which device converts solar energy into electrical energy?
questions.answer: Photovoltaic cell

questions.text: State two advantages of wind energy.
questions.answer: 1. It is a renewable and clean source of energy. 2. Wind turbines have low operational costs once installed.

questions.text: What is biomass? Give an example.
questions.answer: Biomass is organic material obtained from plants and animals used as fuel. Example: Cow dung, agricultural waste.

questions.text: Hydroelectricity is generated using:
questions.answer: Flowing water

questions.text: What is nuclear energy? How is it obtained?
questions.answer: Nuclear energy is the energy released from the nucleus of atoms during nuclear fission or fusion. It is obtained mainly by fission of uranium or plutonium in reactors.

questions.text: Explain the importance of energy conservation.
questions.answer: Energy conservation reduces energy waste, saves natural resources, lowers pollution, and ensures sustainable energy availability for future generations.

questions.text: Explain how electricity is generated using solar energy.
questions.answer: Solar energy is absorbed by photovoltaic (PV) cells made from semiconductor materials like silicon. Sunlight excites electrons, generating electric current. PV modules are connected to form solar panels, which supply usable electricity. Solar farms produce electricity on a large scale.

questions.text: Describe the working of a biogas plant with a labeled diagram.
questions.answer: Biogas plants use anaerobic digestion of biomass such as cow dung and agricultural waste. The mixture is placed in an airtight digester where microbes decompose it, releasing methane-rich biogas. The gas is used as fuel, while the residue works as fertilizer. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Compare conventional and non-conventional energy sources with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Conventional sources such as coal, petroleum, and natural gas are non-renewable, cause pollution, and have limited availability. Non-conventional sources such as solar, wind, tidal, and geothermal are renewable, eco-friendly, and sustainable. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}

questions.text: Atomic power plant in Maharashtra is located at:
questions.answer: Tarapur

questions.text: Observe the given picture and answer questions related to the energy project shown.
questions.answer: The project uses renewable energy; it is eco-friendly as it reduces pollution.

questions.text: Solar photovoltaic cell converts solar radiation directly into:
questions.answer: Electrical

questions.text: Which fuel is used in thermal power plants? Write any two problems associated with it.
questions.answer: Coal; causes air pollution and global warming.

chapters.description: Classification of animals based on body structure, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, and phyla such as Porifera, Coelenterata, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, and Chordata.
learningObjectives: Understand the need for classification of animals.
Differentiate between types of symmetry and germ layers.
Describe major animal phyla with characteristics and examples.
Explain the structure and features of chordates.
Classify animals based on body organization and coelom.

questions.text: What is bilateral symmetry?
questions.answer: Bilateral symmetry is when the body can be divided into two equal halves through only one plane, forming mirror images.

questions.text: Animals with a notochord belong to which group?
questions.answer: Chordata

questions.text: Define coelom. Name its three types.
questions.answer: Coelom is a fluid-filled body cavity between the digestive canal and the body wall. Types: Acoelomate, Pseudocoelomate, and Coelomate.

questions.text: What are germ layers? Name them.
questions.answer: Germ layers are primary layers of cells formed during embryonic development. They are ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.text: Which phylum includes starfish and sea urchins?
questions.answer: Echinodermata

questions.text: State two characteristics of arthropods.
questions.answer: 1. They have jointed appendages. 2. Their body is segmented and covered by an exoskeleton made of chitin.

questions.text: Differentiate between vertebrates and invertebrates.
questions.answer: Vertebrates possess a vertebral column and internal skeleton, while invertebrates lack a vertebral column and have simpler body structures.

questions.text: Explain the characteristics of phylum Chordata.
questions.answer: Chordates possess a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail, and a closed circulatory system. They show bilateral symmetry and are triploblastic coelomates. Examples: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

questions.text: Describe the differences between Mollusca and Echinodermata.
questions.answer: Mollusca: Soft-bodied animals, usually with a calcareous shell; bilateral symmetry; examples include octopus, snails. Echinodermata: Marine organisms with spiny skin; radial symmetry in adults; water vascular system; examples include starfish and sea lilies. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Explain the basis of animal classification using body symmetry, germ layers, and coelom.
questions.answer: Animals are classified based on: 1. Body symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (cnidarians), bilateral (arthropods, chordates). 2. Germ layers: diploblastic (two layers) or triploblastic (three layers). 3. Coelom: acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, or coelomate. These features indicate evolutionary complexity. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}

questions.text: Example of phylum Arthropoda is:
questions.answer: Scorpion

questions.text: Identify the phylum based on given characteristics.
questions.answer: Echinodermata, Nematoda and Pisces identified correctly with examples.

questions.text: Distinguish between Class Pisces and Class Reptiles.
questions.answer: Pisces breathe through gills; reptiles breathe through lungs. Pisces are aquatic; reptiles mostly terrestrial.

questions.text: Write three characteristics of phylum Mollusca.
questions.answer: Soft body, muscular foot, mantle present.

chapters.title: Introduction to Microbiology
chapters.description: Microorganisms, their characteristics, industrial applications, biotechnology, antibiotics, vaccines, fermentation, biofertilizers, and microbial ecology.
learningObjectives: Identify major groups of microorganisms and their characteristics.
Explain industrial applications of microbes such as fermentation and antibiotic production.
Understand vaccines, immunity, and microbial diseases.
Describe the role of microorganisms in agriculture and environment.
Explain biotechnology and its applications.

questions.text: What are microorganisms?
questions.answer: Microorganisms are tiny living organisms such as bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae, and viruses that are too small to be seen with the naked eye.

questions.text: Which microorganism is used in the production of curd?
questions.answer: Lactobacillus

questions.text: Define fermentation. Give one example.
questions.answer: Fermentation is a metabolic process in which microorganisms convert sugars into alcohol or acids. Example: Yeast ferments sugar to produce alcohol.

questions.text: What are antibiotics?
questions.answer: Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by microorganisms that inhibit or destroy harmful microbes. Example: Penicillin.

questions.text: Which microorganism increases soil fertility by nitrogen fixation?
questions.answer: Rhizobium

questions.text: What is biotechnology?
questions.answer: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products to develop useful materials, medicines, and technologies. It includes genetic engineering, fermentation, and industrial microbiology.

questions.text: State two uses of microorganisms in industry.
questions.answer: 1. Production of antibiotics such as penicillin. 2. Fermentation processes to make wine, beer, vinegar, and cheese.

questions.text: Explain how vaccines work. Give an example.
questions.answer: Vaccines contain weakened or inactive pathogens that stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies. This creates immunity without causing disease. Example: Polio vaccine trains the body to fight poliovirus.

questions.text: Describe the role of microorganisms in agriculture.
questions.answer: Microorganisms such as Rhizobium fix atmospheric nitrogen in soil. Cyanobacteria enrich soil fertility. Decomposers break down organic matter, improving soil nutrients. Biopesticides derived from microbes control pests naturally. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

questions.text: Explain industrial production of antibiotics with reference to Penicillin.
questions.answer: Penicillin is produced by cultivating Penicillium fungus in large fermenters under controlled conditions. After fermentation, the antibiotic is extracted, purified, and prepared for medicinal use. This process revolutionized treatment of bacterial infections.

questions.text: Lactobacillus brevis gives us the beverage:
questions.answer: Cider

questions.text: Name two fuels obtained by microbial processes. Why should their use be increased?
questions.answer: Biogas and ethanol; they are renewable and eco-friendly.

questions.text: Vinegar contains which acid?
questions.answer: Acetic

questions.text: Explain types of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms with examples.
questions.answer: Binary fission in Amoeba; multiple fission in Plasmodium.

chapters.title: Cell Biology and Biotechnology
chapters.description: Genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, gene therapy, stem cells, transgenic organisms, bioinformatics, and applications of biotechnology.
learningObjectives: Explain the process and purpose of genetic engineering.
Understand recombinant DNA technology and its applications.
Describe cloning, stem cells, and gene therapy.
Differentiate between types of stem cells.
Explain importance of bioinformatics in biotechnology.

questions.text: What is genetic engineering?
questions.answer: Genetic engineering is the technique of manipulating an organism’s DNA to change or introduce characteristics by adding, removing, or modifying genes.

questions.text: Which enzyme is used to cut DNA at specific sites?
questions.answer: Restriction endonuclease

questions.text: What is recombinant DNA?
questions.answer: Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by combining genes from two different organisms using enzymes like restriction endonucleases and ligases.

questions.text: Explain cloning with an example.
questions.answer: Cloning is producing genetically identical copies of organisms. Example: Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned using a somatic cell.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an application of biotechnology?
questions.answer: Formation of fossils

questions.text: What are stem cells? Name their two main types.
questions.answer: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells capable of division and differentiation. Types: 1. Embryonic stem cells, 2. Adult stem cells.

questions.text: Explain gene therapy.
questions.answer: Gene therapy is a technique that involves inserting a normal gene into cells in place of a defective one to treat genetic disorders.

questions.text: Describe the steps involved in recombinant DNA technology.
questions.answer: Steps include: 1. Isolation of desired gene. 2. Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes. 3. Insertion of gene into vector DNA. 4. Ligation using DNA ligase. 5. Transfer of recombinant DNA into host organism. 6. Expression of new gene to produce desired protein.

questions.text: Explain the importance of biotechnology in agriculture and medicine.
questions.answer: In agriculture, biotechnology helps produce pest-resistant crops, increase yield, and improve nutritional quality. In medicine, it enables production of vaccines, insulin, antibiotics, gene therapy, and diagnosis through DNA fingerprinting.

questions.text: What is bioinformatics? Explain its applications.
questions.answer: Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to manage and analyze biological data such as DNA sequences. Applications include genome mapping, drug development, studying protein structures, and disease diagnosis.

questions.text: What is DNA fingerprinting? Where is it mainly useful?
questions.answer: DNA fingerprinting is a technique to identify individuals using DNA patterns; used in forensic science.

questions.text: Give any two commercial uses of biotechnology.
questions.answer: Production of insulin and vaccines.

questions.text: What is stem cell? Write any four uses of stem cell.
questions.answer: Stem cells can divide and differentiate. Used in regenerative medicine, cancer treatment, tissue repair and research.

learningObjectives: Explain the meaning and importance of social and mental health.
Understand addiction, its consequences, and prevention.
Identify factors that affect socially healthy behavior.
Learn methods of stress management and emotional balance.
Recognize the importance of family, friends, and support systems.

questions.text: What is social health?
questions.answer: Social health is the ability of a person to form satisfying interpersonal relationships and adapt comfortably to different social situations.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sign of good mental health?
questions.answer: Self-confidence

questions.text: State any two factors that affect social health.
questions.answer: 1. Family environment. 2. Peer relationships. 3. Economic conditions. 4. Education and lifestyle.

questions.text: What is addiction? Give one example.
questions.answer: Addiction is a mental or physical dependence on substances or activities that affect normal life. Example: addiction to alcohol or drugs.

questions.text: Which of the following is a healthy coping mechanism for stress?
questions.answer: Physical exercise

questions.text: Explain the role of family in maintaining social health.
questions.answer: Family provides emotional support, teaches values, and helps develop communication and problem-solving skills, all of which contribute to social well-being.

questions.text: What are lifestyle diseases? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Lifestyle diseases arise from unhealthy habits such as poor diet, inactivity, and stress. Examples: diabetes, hypertension, heart disease.

questions.text: Explain the effects of addiction on personal and social life.
questions.answer: Addiction causes physical illness, emotional instability, financial problems, and poor academic or work performance. It damages relationships, leads to social isolation, and increases crime rates and burden on healthcare systems.

questions.text: Describe the importance of mental health and methods to maintain it.
questions.answer: Mental health ensures emotional balance, decision-making, and productivity. It can be maintained through regular exercise, communication, meditation, time management, seeking counseling, and maintaining healthy relationships.

questions.text: Explain how peer influence can be positive or negative.
questions.answer: Positive peer influence promotes good habits, discipline, motivation, and teamwork. Negative influence may lead to substance abuse, risky behavior, poor academic performance, and emotional stress. Guidance and self-awareness help manage peer influence.

questions.text: Write full form of WHO.
questions.answer: World Health Organization.

questions.text: Write names of any six materials required in a first aid box.
questions.answer: Cotton, antiseptic, bandage, scissors, gauze, adhesive tape.

questions.text: Write any four methods to reduce stress.
questions.answer: Exercise, meditation, proper sleep, time management.

chapters.title: Disaster Management
chapters.description: Types of disasters, disaster preparedness, mitigation, relief measures, first aid, rescue operations, and roles of government and community.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between natural and man-made disasters.
Explain disaster preparedness and mitigation techniques.
Understand the importance of rescue operations and first aid.
Identify government and community roles in disaster management.
Describe steps to reduce disaster risks.

questions.text: What is a disaster?
questions.answer: A disaster is a sudden event that causes extensive damage to life, property, and the environment, disrupting normal functioning of communities.

questions.text: Which of the following is a natural disaster?
questions.answer: Earthquake

questions.text: What is disaster preparedness?
questions.answer: Disaster preparedness includes planning, training, and taking precautions to reduce loss of life and property during disasters through early warning systems, drills, and resource readiness.

questions.text: State two differences between natural and man-made disasters.
questions.answer: Natural disasters occur due to natural processes (earthquakes, floods), while man-made disasters result from human activities (industrial accidents, bomb blasts). Their causes, predictability, and mitigation methods vary.

questions.text: What should be the first step in first aid?
options: Ensure safety of victim and rescuer
questions.answer: Ensure safety of victim and rescuer

questions.text: Define mitigation. Give an example.
questions.answer: Mitigation refers to long-term measures taken to reduce disaster risks, such as building earthquake-resistant structures or constructing flood-control dams.

questions.text: Explain the importance of community participation during disasters.
questions.answer: Community members provide immediate help, communicate early warnings, participate in rescue operations, donate resources, and support rehabilitation efforts, reducing overall damage.

questions.text: Describe the steps involved in rescue operations during disasters.
questions.answer: Rescue operations involve: 1. Assessing the situation and ensuring safety. 2. Mobilizing trained teams. 3. Removing victims from danger zones. 4. Providing first aid. 5. Transporting injured individuals to hospitals. 6. Coordinating with fire, medical, and police departments.

questions.text: Explain the role of government agencies in disaster management.
questions.answer: Government agencies establish disaster management authorities, create early warning systems, coordinate rescue teams, supply essential materials, run rehabilitation programs, enforce safety laws, and train communities through awareness programs.

questions.text: What safety measures should be followed during an earthquake?
questions.answer: Safety measures include: staying away from windows, taking shelter under sturdy furniture, turning off electricity and gas, avoiding elevators, moving to open spaces, and following evacuation routes. Buildings should be earthquake-resistant to reduce risk.

questions.text: Write four adverse effects of radiations on human body.
questions.answer: Cancer, genetic mutations, skin damage, radiation sickness.

questions.text: Observe the given picture and write any two effects of the disaster.
questions.answer: Loss of life and property; environmental damage.

questions.text: Write reasons, effects and remedial measures of any one disaster seen or heard by you.
questions.answer: Earthquake: caused by tectonic movement; effects include destruction; remedies include preparedness and safe construction.

questions.text: Define a linear equation in two variables with an example.
questions.answer: An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0 where a, b, and c are real numbers and a, b are not both zero is a linear equation in two variables. Example: 2x + 3y - 6 = 0.

questions.text: Which of the following is a solution of the equation 2x + y = 7?
Find any two solutions of the equation x − 2y = 4.
questions.answer: Some solutions are (4, 0), (6, 1), (8, 2), etc. (Any two are correct.)

questions.text: If the cost of 1 pen is ₹x and the cost of 1 pencil is ₹y, write the linear equation representing a total expense of ₹50.
questions.answer: The required linear equation is x + y = 50 (or ax + by = 50 depending on quantities).

questions.text: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is:
questions.answer: A straight line

questions.text: Plot the points (0, 3) and (2, -1). What can be said about the line passing through them?
questions.answer: Both points lie on a unique straight line which represents a linear equation in two variables.

questions.text: Write intercepts of the equation 3x + 6y = 12.
questions.answer: x-intercept = 4 (when y = 0), y-intercept = 2 (when x = 0).

questions.text: Draw the graph of the equation x + 2y = 6. Identify any two points on the graph and determine whether (2, 2) lies on it.
questions.answer: Taking values: y=0 → x=6 gives (6, 0); y=1 → x=4 gives (4, 1). Plotting these gives a straight line. Substituting (2,2): 2 + 4 = 6 ✓, hence (2,2) lies on the line.

questions.text: A fruit seller sells apples at ₹x per kg and oranges at ₹y per kg. On a particular day, he sold 5 kg apples and 8 kg oranges for a total of ₹760. Form the linear equation. If apples cost ₹40/kg, find the price of oranges.
questions.answer: Linear equation: 5x + 8y = 760. Substituting x = 40: 200 + 8y = 760 → 8y = 560 → y = 70. Oranges cost ₹70/kg.

questions.text: Explain why a linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions. Support your answer using an example.
questions.answer: A linear equation in two variables represents a straight line, and every point on that line is a solution. Thus, infinitely many ordered pairs satisfy it. Example: For x + y = 5, pairs like (1,4), (2,3), (3,2) etc. are all valid, and the list is infinite.

questions.text: If 2x + y = 7 and x + 2y = 11, then find the value of x + y.
questions.answer: Solve system: from 2x+y=7 and x+2y=11 → multiply first by2:4x+2y=14 subtract second:3x–? (Better direct): Solve: Multiply first by2:4x+2y=14; subtract (x+2y=11) → 3x=3 → x=1. Then y=7–2x=5. So x+y=6.

questions.text: Complete the following table to draw the graph of x + 2y = 4. (Given x = -2, y = 1 and fill the (x,y) pair column.)
questions.answer: Substitute given x values into x+2y=4 to find corresponding y (or given). For example, for x = -2: -2 + 2y = 4 → 2y = 6 → y = 3, so point (-2,3). (Complete remaining entries similarly.)

The triangle on X-axis between x=1 and x=6; area = ½ × base × height where height is y at intersection? (Compute intersection of the two lines to get vertex; then compute area). questions.text: Define a quadratic equation with an example.
questions.answer: A quadratic equation is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. Example: 2x² + 5x - 3 = 0.

The length of a rectangle is 3 m more than its breadth. If the area is 70 m², form the quadratic equation and find its dimensions.
questions.answer: Let breadth = x; length = x + 3.   x(x + 3) = 70 → x² + 3x - 70 = 0.  Solving: x = 7 or x = -10. Negative rejected. Breadth = 7 m, Length = 10 m.

questions.text: Explain how the nature of roots of a quadratic equation is determined using the discriminant. Give examples.
questions.answer: If D = b² - 4ac: • D > 0 → real and distinct roots (e.g., x² - 5x + 6 = 0).  • D = 0 → real and equal roots (e.g., x² - 4x + 4 = 0).   • D < 0 → non-real/imaginary roots (e.g., x² + x + 1 = 0).

questions.text: From the following equations which one is a quadratic equation?
questions.answer: (C) n² − n − 12 is a quadratic equation (in n).

questions.text: Complete the activity to form a quadratic equation: I am a quadratic equation. My roots are 5 and 12. Fill: Sum of roots, Product of roots, My quadratic equation is ____.
questions.answer: Sum = 17, Product = 60. Quadratic equation: x² − 17x + 60 = 0.

questions.text: Solve the quadratic equation by factorisation: m² + 14m + 13 = 0.
Solve the quadratic equation by using formula method: x² − 2x − 3 = 0.
questions.answer: Use quadratic formula or factor: x² −2x −3 = (x−3)(x+1) → x = 3 or x = −1.

questions.text: Find the value of m if the quadratic equation (m − 12)x² + 2(m − 12)x + 2 = 0 has real and equal roots.
questions.answer: For real and equal roots discriminant = 0. Here a = m−12, b = 2(m−12), c = 2. Δ = b² − 4ac = [2(m−12)]² − 4(m−12)(2) = 4(m−12)² −8(m−12) = 4(m−12)[(m−12) −2] = 4(m−12)(m−14) = 0. So m = 12 or m = 14. But if a = 0 (m=12) then equation degenerates; check validity. So m = 14 gives genuine equal roots; m = 12 yields linear equation.

questions.text: Define an arithmetic progression (AP).
questions.answer: A sequence is called an arithmetic progression if the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant. This constant is called the common difference.

questions.text: What is the common difference of the AP 7, 10, 13, 16, …?

questions.answer: Given: T₅ = a + 4d = 22 T₁₅ = a + 14d = 52 Subtract: 10d = 30 → d = 3 Substitute: a + 12 = 22 → a = 10.

questions.text: A worker earns ₹800 in the first month and gets a raise of ₹50 every month. How much will he earn in the 12th month? What will be his total earning in 12 months?
Explain why the sequence formed by the total distance travelled by a car each hour at constant speed is an AP. Give an example.
questions.answer: At constant speed, equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, so the total distance increases by a fixed amount each hour. Example: At 50 km/h: distances = 50, 100, 150, 200… (AP with d = 50).

questions.text: Find the common difference of the following A.P.: 4, 4, 4, ...
questions.answer: 0 (sequence is constant; common difference is 0).

questions.text: Find the first term of the sequence t_n = 3n − 4.

questions.text: Find the 19th term of the following A.P.: 7, 13, 19, 25, ...

A farmer borrows ₹1,000 and agrees to repay with a total interest of ₹140 in 12 instalments. Each instalment is less than the preceding instalment by ₹10. What should be the amount of his first and last instalment?
questions.answer: Total repayment = 1000 + 140 = 1140. Let first instalment = a, common difference between terms = −10, number of terms n = 12. Sum S_n = n/2 [2a + (n−1)d] = 1140. So 12/2 [2a + 11(−10)] =1140 →6[2a −110] =1140 →2a −110 =190 →2a =300 →a =150. Last instalment = a + (n−1)d = 150 +11(−10) = 150 −110 = 40.

questions.text: For an A.P., t₇ = 4 and d = −4. Find the first term a.
Find the first term of the sequence tₙ = 3n − 2.
questions.answer: First term = 1.

questions.text: Find the 19th term of the A.P. 7, 13, 19, 25, …
questions.answer: 19th term = 115.

questions.answer: AP with a = 20, d = 20, n = 29. Total saving = ₹8700.

questions.text: Define probability.
questions.answer: Probability is the measure of the likelihood of an event occurring and is given by: P(E) = (Number of favourable outcomes) / (Total number of possible outcomes).

questions.text: What is the probability of getting a tail when tossing a fair coin?

questions.answer: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6 → 2 favourable outcomes. Total outcomes = 6 → Probability = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.text: A bag contains 3 red balls and 5 blue balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability of drawing a blue ball.

questions.text: If P(A) = 0.7, then P(A') (complement of A) is:

questions.answer: There are 4 kings in the deck → Probability = 4/52 = 1/13.

questions.text: Find the probability of getting an even number when a die is rolled.
questions.answer: Even numbers: 2, 4, 6 → 3 favourable outcomes. Probability = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.text: The probability that a student passes an exam is 0.78. What is the probability that the student fails? Also interpret the meaning.

questions.text: A number is chosen randomly from the numbers 1 to 30. Find the probability that the number is (a) a multiple of 3, (b) a prime number.

questions.text: A two-digit number is to be formed from the digits 2, 3, 5 without repetition. Find the probability that the number formed is odd. (Complete activity: list S and A.)

questions.text: A student scored the following marks in 6 tests: 35, 40, 50, 45, 55, 65. Find the mean, median, and mode.

chapters.description: Properties of similar triangles, tests of similarity, basic proportionality theorem, ratio of areas, and applications.

learningObjectives: Understand the meaning of similarity and criteria for similar triangles.
